::: notes
From DSCI 221's "The Dictionary Problem" slide.

There's no answer: in an arbitrary tree, 25 could be anywhere, so find has
to look at every node -- Θ(n), no better than a list. And 37 could go
anywhere, which is the same problem in reverse.

So the tree needs a rule about *where keys live*. Next slide: a tree that
has one -- see if you can work out what it is.
:::

Try:

2. **insert(40)**: 38 → 51 → left of 51. There is exactly one place it can go.

::: {.column width="45%"}
A **Binary Search Tree (BST)** is a binary tree, T, such that:

- \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_, OR
- T = {r, T<sub>L</sub>, T<sub>R</sub>} and

  x ∈ T<sub>L</sub> → \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

  x ∈ T<sub>R</sub> → \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

and
:::
::::

::: notes
- T is **empty**, OR
- T = {r, T_L, T_R} and
  - x ∈ T_L → **x.key < r.key**
  - x ∈ T_R → **x.key > r.key**
- **and** T_L and T_R are BSTs.

The "and" matters: checking only each node against its own children is not
enough. 37 sits right of 25 — fine — but it must also be less than 38,
because it's in 38's left subtree.
:::

```cpp
template<class K, class D>
class Dictionary {
```

::: notes
Three nodes have lost their keys. What could each one be? The left child of
13 must be less than 13; the right child of 25 must be between 25 and 38;
the left child of 84 between 51 and 84. A key's position constrains it from
*every* ancestor.

Each node now carries a **key** (what we search by) and **data** (what we
want back) — the locker number and the name.

What if `key == croot->key`?

\

Running time:
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```cpp
template<class K>
void insert(Node * croot, const K & key) {

    if (croot == nullptr)
        croot = new Node(key);

    else if (key < croot->key)
        insert(croot->left);

    else if (key > croot->key)
        insert(croot->right);
}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Insert 95 (or any key): walk down as if finding it, and hang the new node
where the search falls off the tree.

`key == croot->key`: the key is already there. Either do nothing, or
replace the data — keys are unique.

Running time: **Θ(h)**, one step per level, where h is the height.

Does this code work? Two problems:

1. `croot` is passed **by value**. `croot = new Node(key)` changes the copy;
   the parent's pointer is still null and the new node leaks.
2. `insert(croot->left)` forgets the key.

```
void insert(Node *& croot, const K & key) {   // & on the pointer
    if (croot == nullptr) croot = new Node(key);
    else if (key < croot->key) insert(croot->left, key);
    else if (key > croot->key) insert(croot->right, key);
}
```
:::

Pick **A** or **B** at random. On paper, insert those keys **in that order** into an empty BST.

:::: {.columns}

4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**B**

1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
:::
::::

\

Then find someone who picked the **other** list, and compare.

- Same keys, same `insert` code. What's different?
- Which tree would you rather run `find(7)` on?

::: notes
About 3 minutes. Adapted from DSCI 221's "Building a BST" and its practice
problems.

A gives a perfect tree, height 2. B gives a stick going right,
height 6: every insert walks the whole chain.

Check both in the explorer (Clear, then Insert each key) so the room sees
them.

find(7): 3 steps vs 7. Same keys, same code -- the *insertion order*
decided the height, and the running time is Θ(h). Plant the question for
the end of the lesson ("How fast?") and for Wednesday: can we make sure we
always get the left tree?
:::

```cpp
template<class K>
Node *& find_(K & key, Node *& r) {

    if (r == nullptr)


    else if (r->key == key)


    else if


    else

}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
```
if (r == nullptr)            return r;
else if (r->key == key)      return r;
else if (key < r->key)       return find_(key, r->left);
else                         return find_(key, r->right);
```

Why return `Node *&`? It hands back the **pointer itself** — the parent's
`left` or `right`, or `root`. If the key isn't there, that pointer is the
null one where the key belongs, so insert becomes
`Node *& p = find_(key, root); if (p == nullptr) p = new Node(key, data);`.

Running time: **Θ(h)**.
:::

```cpp
void BST<K>::remove(Node *& croot, const K & k) {
    if (croot != nullptr) {
        if (croot->key == key)
            doRemoval(cRoot);
        else if (k < croot->key)
            remove(cRoot->left, k);
        else
            remove(cRoot->right, k);
    }
}
```

```cpp

        _____ChildRemove(cRoot);

        _____ChildRemove(cRoot);
}
```

```cpp
void BST<K>::zeroOneChildRemove(Node * & cRoot) {
    Node * temp = cRoot;
    if (cRoot->left == nullptr) cRoot = cRoot->right;
    else cRoot = cRoot->left;
    delete temp;
}
```

::: notes
`cRoot` is a reference to the parent's pointer, so reassigning it splices
the node out. If the left child is null, the right child (possibly also
null — the leaf case) moves up; otherwise the left does. Then free the old
node. Both the zero- and one-child cases in five lines.
:::

Running time of Dictionary functions?

Which traversal sorts the keys?

What's left?

::: notes
- find and insert are **Θ(h)**. For n keys, h is somewhere between
  $\log n$ (bushy) and $n - 1$ (a stick — insert keys in sorted order).
  So: $O(\log n)$ if we're lucky, $O(n)$ if we're not.
- **Inorder** visits the keys in sorted order.
- remove (so far) is **Θ(h)** too.
- Left: removing a node with **two** children (next time), and keeping the
  tree short so we're always lucky.
:::
